blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Picture two spreadsheets that both already use the same employee ID as their row labels. If they are lined up that way, stapling them together is trivial: row one meets row one, row two meets row two, and you never had to look anything up by name. That is basically what join() does for you in pandas. It combines two DataFrames using their row index instead of asking you to name a column, which makes it the natural choice whenever your data already has that kind of meaningful, aligned index sitting there ready to use.

You already know merge(), which is the general purpose tool for combining DataFrames on shared columns. join() is not a separate, competing idea. It solves the exact same problem from a different starting point, and by the end of this lesson you will see it is really just a shortcut for a very specific, very common kind of merge.

blocks.alt: A left DataFrame and a right DataFrame both feeding into a join node that matches them by index label, producing a combined DataFrame
blocks.caption: join lines rows up by index label, not by a named column.

blocks.text: Here is the contrast in miniature. Notice which one has to name a column and which one does not.

code.content:
# merge needs you to name the columns to line up on
orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id")

# join just uses whatever index each DataFrame already has
orders.join(customers)

blocks.title: Same join types, different backdrop
blocks.content: left, right, outer, and inner mean exactly the same thing here as they did with merge. What is genuinely different about join is not that vocabulary, it is the default value pandas picks for you, and where it expects the join key to live. Keep that framing in mind for the rest of this lesson.

blocks.text: 2. Join by Index: The Default Behavior

Call df1.join(df2) with no extra arguments and pandas lines up rows by comparing the index of df1 against the index of df2. Wherever an index value shows up on both sides, the columns from both DataFrames land in the same row. There is no column name to pass, because the index already is the thing being matched.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame(
    {"amount": [250, 90, 430]},
    index=pd.Index(["C1", "C2", "C3"], name="customer_id"),
)
customers = pd.DataFrame(
    {"name": ["Ravi", "Meera", "Aditya"]},
    index=pd.Index(["C1", "C2", "C3"], name="customer_id"),
)

print(orders.join(customers))
#              amount    name
# customer_id
# C1              250    Ravi
# C2               90   Meera
# C3              430  Aditya

blocks.alt: Three pairs of matching index labels, C1, C2, and C3, from a left DataFrame lined up against the same labels on a right DataFrame
blocks.caption: Every matching index label on both sides becomes one combined row.

blocks.text: 2.1 Setting a Meaningful Index First

join earns its keep specifically once one or both of your DataFrames already have a meaningful index, usually because you called set_index() on a shared ID column earlier in your pipeline. If your data is still sitting on the default 0, 1, 2 integer index, joining by index is not useful yet, since those numbers do not mean anything across the two DataFrames.
3. The how Parameter: Join Defaults to Left, Not Inner

join accepts the same how values you already used with merge: left, right, outer, and inner, and they mean exactly the same thing here. What actually matters is the default pandas picks when you leave how out entirely, because merge and join do not agree with each other.

blocks.title: The default that flips on you
blocks.content: merge defaults to how equals inner. join defaults to how equals left. Write the same code with each and you can get a different number of rows back, purely because of that one default. This is genuinely worth memorizing, because it is the single easiest way to get quietly surprised by pandas.

blocks.alt: df.join other pointing to how equals left by default, next to df.merge other pointing to how equals inner by default
blocks.caption: join keeps unmatched left rows by default. merge drops them by default.

code.content:
left = pd.DataFrame({"score": [10, 20, 30]}, index=["a", "b", "c"])
right = pd.DataFrame({"grade": ["A", "B"]}, index=["a", "b"])

print(left.join(right))
#    score grade
# a     10     A
# b     20     B
# c     30   NaN     <- row c survives, join defaults to how="left"

print(left.merge(right, left_index=True, right_index=True))
#    score grade
# a     10     A
# b     20     B
#                     <- row c is gone, merge defaults to how="inner"

blocks.text: 3.1 Overriding how When You Need To
Nothing stops you from passing how explicitly to join, same as you would with merge. If you only want rows whose index shows up on both sides, ask for it directly.

code.content:
print(left.join(right, how="inner"))
#    score grade
# a     10     A
# b     20     B

blocks.text: 4. Joining a Column Against Another DataFrame’s Index With on

Sometimes the calling DataFrame still has your ID sitting in a regular column, not the index, while the other DataFrame already has that same ID set as its index. The on parameter covers exactly that case: it tells join which column of the calling DataFrame to match against the index of the other one, without you having to call set_index() first.

blocks.alt: A customer_id column on the orders DataFrame pointing through on equals customer_id at the index of the customers DataFrame, producing a joined result
blocks.caption: on points a column on the calling side at the index on the other side.

code.content:
orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "customer_id": ["C1", "C2", "C1"],
    "amount": [250, 90, 430],
})
customers = pd.DataFrame(
    {"name": ["Ravi", "Meera"]},
    index=pd.Index(["C1", "C2"], name="customer_id"),
)

print(orders.join(customers, on="customer_id"))
#    order_id customer_id  amount   name
# 0       101          C1     250   Ravi
# 1       102          C2      90  Meera
# 2       103          C1     430   Ravi

blocks.title: on only looks one way
blocks.content: on always means a column on the calling DataFrame matched against the index on the other DataFrame. It cannot point at a column on the other side too. If you need column to column matching where the column names differ on each side, that is exactly what merge’s left_on and right_on were built for.

blocks.text: 5. Under the Hood: join Is Built on merge

join is not a second, independent engine living alongside merge. It is a thin convenience wrapper that pandas built specifically for the index based case, and internally it hands the real work off to merge with a particular set of arguments already filled in for you.

blocks.alt: You calling df.join other, flowing into join building arguments, flowing into pd.merge running underneath, flowing into the result coming back
blocks.caption: join quietly calls merge for you with the index arguments already set.

code.content:
# roughly what happens when you write this
orders.join(customers)

# is equivalent, under the hood, to this
orders.merge(customers, left_index=True, right_index=True, how="left")

blocks.text: That equivalence is the whole story. Anything join can do, you could always write out by hand as a merge call with the right combination of left_index, right_index, on, and how. join just saves you the typing for the pattern that comes up constantly: two frames, aligned indexes, done.
6. Overlapping Columns: lsuffix and rsuffix

If both DataFrames have a column with the same name that is not the join key, pandas needs a way to keep them apart in the result. merge solves this with a single suffixes argument, a tuple of two strings. join solves the identical problem with two separate keyword arguments, lsuffix and rsuffix, one string each.

blocks.alt: A status column on the left DataFrame gaining an lsuffix to become status_order, and a status column on the right gaining an rsuffix to become status_shipment, both flowing into the joined DataFrame
blocks.caption: lsuffix and rsuffix rename only the colliding columns, one string per side.

code.content:
left = pd.DataFrame({"status": ["open", "closed"]}, index=["o1", "o2"])
right = pd.DataFrame({"status": ["shipped", "pending"]}, index=["o1", "o2"])

combined = left.join(right, lsuffix="_order", rsuffix="_shipment")
print(combined)
#    status_order status_shipment
# o1         open         shipped
# o2       closed         pending

blocks.title: Two strings, not one tuple
blocks.content: This trips people up moving between the two methods. merge takes suffixes as a single tuple argument, suffixes=("_x", "_y"). join takes the exact same idea as two completely separate keyword arguments, lsuffix and rsuffix. Same job, different calling convention, and Python will not warn you if you mix them up, it will just raise a confusing error about an unexpected keyword.

blocks.text: 7. Joining Three or More DataFrames at Once

Pass a list of DataFrames to join instead of a single one, and pandas lines all of them up against the calling DataFrame’s index in one call. merge cannot do this directly. merge only ever combines two objects at a time, so combining three DataFrames with merge means chaining two separate merge calls.

blocks.alt: Orders, customers, and regions DataFrames all feeding into one join node, producing one combined DataFrame
blocks.caption: A list of DataFrames, one join call, everything lined up on the shared index.

code.content:
orders = pd.DataFrame({"amount": [250, 90, 430]}, index=pd.Index(["C1", "C2", "C3"], name="customer_id"))
customers = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Ravi", "Meera", "Aditya"]}, index=pd.Index(["C1", "C2", "C3"], name="customer_id"))
regions = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["West", "South", "North"]}, index=pd.Index(["C1", "C2", "C3"], name="customer_id"))

all_together = orders.join([customers, regions])
print(all_together)
#              amount    name region
# customer_id
# C1              250    Ravi   West
# C2               90   Meera  South
# C3              430  Aditya  North

blocks.title: lsuffix and rsuffix stop working here
blocks.content: Once you pass a list instead of a single DataFrame, lsuffix and rsuffix are no longer available to resolve collisions. If any of the DataFrames in the list share a column name, pandas raises an error instead of guessing which suffix goes where. Rename the colliding columns yourself before joining a list of more than two frames.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: Shared ID Index, Join vs Merge Side by Side

Let’s put the whole relationship in one place. You will build two small DataFrames, give them a shared ID index, join them, then write the equivalent merge call and confirm you land on the exact same result.

blocks.alt: Orders and customers DataFrames both having called set_index on customer_id, sharing that same index
blocks.caption: Both DataFrames now share customer_id as a real, meaningful index.

code.content:
joined = orders.join(customers)
print(joined)
#              amount    name
# customer_id
# C1              250    Ravi
# C2               90   Meera
# C3              430  Aditya
# C4              120     NaN     <- kept, because how="left" is the default

blocks.alt: orders.join customers and orders.merge customers matched on index both arrows pointing to the same identical result
blocks.caption: Write it as merge with left_index and right_index and you get the identical table back.

code.content:
merged = orders.merge(customers, left_index=True, right_index=True, how="left")
print(merged)
#              amount    name
# customer_id
# C1              250    Ravi
# C2               90   Meera
# C3              430  Aditya
# C4              120     NaN

blocks.title: Same table, two spellings
blocks.content: joined and merged above are identical, column for column, row for row. That is not a coincidence, it is the wrapper relationship from section 5 playing out with real data. join simply saved you from writing left_index=True, right_index=True, and how="left" by hand.

blocks.text: 9. join vs merge: When to Reach for Which
Both tools end up in the same place, so the real question is which one gets you there with less friction for the situation you are actually in.

blocks.alt: A decision diamond asking whether both DataFrames already share a meaningful index, branching to use join for yes and use merge for no
blocks.caption: When the indexes are already aligned, join is less typing for the same result.

blocks.text: 9.1 Reach for join When

items: Both DataFrames already have a meaningful, aligned index, usually right after you called set_index on a shared ID column.
You want the shortest possible call for the common case of lining rows up by that shared index.
You are combining more than two DataFrames at once and they all share the same index, since join accepts a list and merge does not.

blocks.text: 9.2 Reach for merge When

items: You are working with columns directly and have not set a meaningful index yet.
The two DataFrames use differently named columns for the same key, so you need left_on and right_on to bridge them.
You want the validate parameter to catch an unexpected one to many or many to many relationship before it silently duplicates rows.
You are combining exactly two DataFrames and the natural join key already lives in a column, not the index.

blocks.alt: join summarized as index based with how left and lsuffix rsuffix, next to merge summarized as column based with how inner and a suffixes tuple
blocks.caption: The two methods side by side, the same job, two different entry points.

blocks.text: 10. Wrapping Up

join and merge solve the same problem: combining two DataFrames into one. The difference is where each one starts. merge starts from columns you name explicitly. join starts from whatever index each DataFrame already has, which makes it the fast path once you have already set up a meaningful, aligned index with set_index.

items: join lines up rows by index by default, not by a column, which is the opposite starting point from merge.
how defaults to left for join and inner for merge. Mixing that up is the single most common surprise people run into.
on lets a column on the calling DataFrame match against the index of the other DataFrame, but only in that direction.
join is a thin convenience wrapper around merge, so anything join can do, an equivalent merge call can also do.
join can combine more than two DataFrames in one call by passing a list. merge only ever combines two at a time.

blocks.title: Where this goes next
blocks.content: Combining DataFrames side by side is only half the picture. The next lessons cover stacking DataFrames on top of each other with concat, then reshaping and summarizing what you have joined together with groupby and aggregation.
